title: ACGME Compliant Residency Schedules Without New Software
description: What the ACGME work hour rules require of a residency schedule, why spreadsheets miss pattern violations, and how programs hand the build to a service.
content:
Summary

  • Every program schedules differently. Some of the rules come from the ACGME. Most do not: which attendings cover which weeks, who cannot be on call the same night as someone else, the rotation one subspecialty will not move, the requests people put in months ago.
  • Fitting all of it together at once is the hard part, and it is why building a schedule by hand takes weeks and why spreadsheets miss the pattern violations.
  • Scheduling Wizard is a managed service: a team that builds physician schedules and nothing else. You send us your rules and requests; we send back the finished schedules. There is no software for your team to learn.

You have inherited the job of building your program's block, call and clinic schedules. If you are an incoming chief resident, or a program director who has taken this on, that means collecting everyone's requests, working out coverage, and fitting rules that mostly are not written down anywhere. Most programs we talk to are piecing all of it together by hand. It takes weeks, and next year a new chief starts over.

Here is what the rules require, and then how programs hand the build off.

What ACGME Compliance Actually Requires: The Six Core Rules

There are six ACGME rules, and a schedule has to satisfy all of them at the same time as everything else your program wants. That is what makes building one by hand slow.

1. The 80-Hour Weekly Limit (Averaged Over 4 Weeks)

Residents cannot work more than 80 hours per week, averaged across a rolling 4-week period. Averaging smooths over a heavy week, but a vacation week does not pull it down: the ACGME leaves vacation out of the average, so three heavy weeks are averaged over three weeks.

2. The 24-Hour Continuous Duty Limit

Residents are capped at 24 consecutive hours of clinical and educational work, with up to 4 additional hours permitted for patient safety transitions like handoffs. Critically, no new clinical responsibilities can be assigned during those final 4 hours.

3. Required Days Off

At least one full, uninterrupted 24-hour day off per week, averaged over 4 weeks. A common misunderstanding: a "post-call" day does not automatically qualify. The day must be completely free from all clinical and educational obligations.

4. Minimum Rest Between Shifts

Residents should have eight hours off between scheduled clinical work periods, and must have at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call. Scheduling a mandatory morning conference too soon after an overnight shift is a frequent, often invisible violation.

5. In-House Call Frequency

In-house call must be scheduled no more frequently than every third night, averaged over 4 weeks. At-home call is not subject to that limit, but clinical work done on at-home call counts toward the 80 hours, and at-home call cannot fall on a resident's free day.

6. PGY-1 Resident Limits, Now Following 24+4

Since 2017, PGY-1 residents follow the same 24+4 rule as all other residents: up to 24 continuous hours of clinical work with up to 4 additional hours for transitions of care and education. Previously, PGY-1s were capped at 16 continuous hours. Programs should make sure their schedule templates reflect the current 24+4 standard for all PGY levels.

Subspecialty-Specific Overlays

These six rules are just the foundation. Many subspecialties layer additional requirements on top, surgery programs have case and coverage requirements, family medicine programs must meet continuity clinic attendance thresholds, and anesthesiology programs have their own scheduling rules. These specialty-specific overlays are precisely where manual Excel schedules most reliably fail.

Why Your Excel Spreadsheet Is a Compliance Time Bomb

Manual Excel scheduling isn't just inefficient; it's structurally incapable of handling the complexity of modern ACGME compliance.

A revealing Reddit thread on work hour reporting laid this bare. Residents described how their hospital's tracking software counted all paid time off (vacation, holidays, sick days) as zero-hour workdays.

If a resident worked three 90-hour weeks in February and then took one week of vacation, the software reported a compliant 67.5-hour average. The program looked fine on paper. The ACGME leaves vacation out of the average, so that resident's real average was 90, and they had just worked dangerously over the cap for three consecutive weeks.

What's worse, some GME offices are aware of the problem and, as one commenter put it, "do not intend to fix it." This is the environment many Program Directors are operating in, one where the structural incentives work against accurate compliance tracking, and where the consequences of getting caught fall on the program, not the spreadsheet.

Silos Create Blind Spots

Most programs build their call schedule, block schedule, and clinic schedule in separate files. This makes it nearly impossible to detect cross-schedule conflicts: a resident assigned to continuity clinic at 8 AM the morning after a 24-hour call shift, for example. Each individual file may look fine. The combined reality is a violation.

The Averaging System Conceals Pattern Violations

A schedule can be built in good faith and still be non-compliant. A chief resident who carefully checks each rotation in isolation won't necessarily catch the 4-week rolling average problem until after it's already happened.

As noted by users tracking this pattern, the averaging methodology allows institutions to "advertise resident work hours that are underestimated by over 10%", not through malice, but through the fundamental design of the tracking system.

Institutional Knowledge Walks Out the Door Every July

Chief residents typically serve one-year terms.

All the accumulated knowledge about why certain call patterns were excluded, which residents have specific exceptions, and how the specialty-specific rules were handled, it lives in someone's head, not in the schedule itself. Every July, the new chief starts from scratch, often spending dozens of hours rebuilding something that was already built the year before.

Manual Auditing Is a Statistical Near-Impossibility

A mid-sized residency program with 20 residents across multiple rotations generates a combinatorial space of billions of potential schedule configurations. There is no practical way to manually audit that space for compliance. You're not finding all the violations; you're finding the visible ones.

The result is a program that believes it is compliant, without any mathematical basis for that belief.

A Better Approach: Build the Rules In Rather Than Audit Afterwards

The conceptual shift here is important. Traditional scheduling is a two-step process: build a schedule, then check it for compliance. The problem is that step two, manual auditing, is unreliable at the scale and complexity of residency scheduling.

The alternative is to write every rule down first, the ACGME ones and your own, and build the schedule to all of them at once. Compliance is then a property of how the schedule was made, not something you hope the review catches. There is still a review at the end; it just has far less to find.

For a program director who has spent years wondering what is lurking in the call schedule, that is not a minor improvement.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between checking a schedule and building the rules in?

The key difference is prevention versus detection. Traditional software checks a manually built schedule for potential errors, while building the rules in means the schedule is shaped by them from the start. The review afterwards becomes a check rather than a repair job.

Do we have to replace our current scheduling platform like Amion or QGenda?

No, you do not need to replace your existing tools. Scheduling Wizard builds the schedule and works alongside the platform you already use, where your residents look at it. You receive the finished schedule as Excel or Google Sheets, or on a custom live view we build for you, and it goes into the platform your residents and faculty already know and use.

How do you handle complex subspecialty rules for programs like surgery or anesthesiology?

Subspecialty-specific rules are written down as core rules for each individual program. Whether it’s specific call frequency requirements for neurosurgery, continuity clinic thresholds for family medicine, or unique shift structures in anesthesiology, these are captured during our intake process and treated with the same weight as the core ACGME duty hour limits.

How does the service handle last-minute changes, like a resident leaving or going on leave?

Bigger changes are handled by rebuilding with the new rules. Instead of a chief resident scrambling to find coverage and potentially introducing a new violation, we rebuild the rest of the block with the same rules in place, spreading the uncovered shifts across the remaining residents. Redrafts for bigger changes are part of the service.

Did the February 2026 ACGME revision change the work hour rules?

Less than the headlines suggested. The February 2026 interim revision of the Common Program Requirements did not change the work hour limits; it suspended enforcement of a handful of requirements, including the rotation-specific 88-hour exception, while the ACGME prepares a major revision (a draft was posted for comment in September 2026 with a proposed effective date of July 1, 2028; nothing in it applies yet). The rules a schedule is built to today are the ones in place since the 2017 revision: 80 hours a week averaged over four weeks, with clinical work from home, at-home call activity and moonlighting all counted; no more than 24 hours of continuous scheduled work plus up to four for transitions, at every PGY level; at least 14 hours free after 24 hours of in-house call; one day in seven free, averaged over four weeks, with no at-home call on those days; and in-house call no more often than every third night. We build to the rules in force, and when they change we rebuild to the new ones.

What is the onboarding process like?

The onboarding process is a structured intake where we collect all of your program's specific requirements, rules, and preferences. There is no software for your team to install or learn. We work with your Program Director, Coordinator, or Chief Resident to gather all inputs, which are then written down as your program's rule set, so the knowledge stays with the program.

How much time does handing the build over save chief residents and program coordinators?

Programs that hand us the build typically save dozens of hours of manual work per year. This frees up chief residents and administrative staff to focus on education and program management rather than tedious and error-prone spreadsheet manipulation.

Can this also improve schedule fairness for residents?

Yes, improving fairness is a primary benefit alongside compliance. We build to whatever fairness definition your program uses, spreading weekend calls, holidays and nights as evenly as the rules allow. A study in Neurosurgery found that similar automated scheduling increased residents' perceived schedule fairness from 43% to 95%, significantly boosting morale.
